source_title: Dick Smith Electronics collapse 2016 - administrators' report (McGrathNicol) findings (named journalism reporting the administrators' creditors' report)
publisher_issuer: Administrators McGrathNicol / receivers Ferrier Hodgson; reported via named journalism (SmartCompany, The Conversation/UNSW)
company_context: Dick Smith Electronics was a major Australian and New Zealand consumer-electronics retail chain. After being sold by Woolworths to private equity (Anchorage Capital) and re-floated, it collapsed into voluntary administration and receivership in January 2016, with an administrators' report detailing the causes.
company_size_stage: mid-market / large private-to-public (ASX-listed after PE float)
macro_context: Competitive consumer-electronics retail with thin margins; the failure was driven by inventory and rebate-driven buying decisions and trading losses rather than a single external shock. Administrators McGrathNicol took control on 4 January 2016; Ferrier Hodgson acted as receivers.
evidence_summary: The Dick Smith group collapsed in early January 2016 with debts of close to A$400 million. The administrators (McGrathNicol) reported that creditors faced a shortfall in excess of A$260 million, substantially worse than the A$170 million book value of the group's assets as at 30 June 2015. Accounts to December 2015 showed considerable losses of A$116.7 million in the six months to 31 December 2015, attributed to poorer-than-expected sales and margins, inventory write-downs, lease provisions and other asset impairments. The administrators also pointed to significant trading losses in Q1 FY2016 and very significant supplier and bank commitments. Receivers Ferrier Hodgson sold the online business and IP to Kogan.com for A$2.6 million but could not find a buyer for the retail stores.
owner_decision_context: Management's buying decisions were reportedly driven by supplier rebates rather than genuine customer demand, building up inventory that could not be sold at adequate margins; leadership continued purchasing/expansion while sales and margins deteriorated, compounding losses until liquidity and supplier/bank commitments became unsustainable.
action_taken: After a failed attempt to trade through deteriorating sales and a large inventory overhang, the company entered voluntary administration and receivership on 4 January 2016. Receivers attempted to sell stock and the business; only the online operation and IP were sold (to Kogan for A$2.6m), and the retail stores were wound down with all outlets eventually closed.
outcome_evidence: Administration/receivership in January 2016 with debts ~A$400m, a creditor shortfall >A$260m, and A$116.7m of losses in the prior half-year confirm terminal insolvency driven by inventory/margin mismanagement and working-capital strain, not a recoverable downturn; the chain ceased trading entirely.
source_limitations: WebFetch typically 403s here; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to the administrators' (McGrathNicol) creditors' report as reported by SmartCompany and corroborated by The Conversation/UNSW. The 'rebate-driven buying' characterisation is from the administrators'/analysts' findings as reported, not read by me in the full primary report. Exact final liquidation recoveries evolved post-report.
directly_stated: Collapsed early January 2016 with debts close to A$400m; administrators McGrathNicol appointed 4 January 2016
Creditor shortfall in excess of A$260m vs A$170m book asset value (30 June 2015)
Losses of A$116.7m in the six months to 31 December 2015 from poor sales/margins, inventory write-downs and impairments
Receivers Ferrier Hodgson sold the online business and IP to Kogan.com for A$2.6m
inferred: Rebate-driven inventory buying disconnected purchasing from real demand, creating an unsellable stock overhang and margin collapse
Working-capital strain plus supplier/bank commitments turned an inventory problem into terminal insolvency
why_useful_for_opsiq: Non-US (Australia/NZ) mid-market retail insolvency with a formal administrators' record, centred on inventory-forecasting mismatch and working-capital stress. Tests whether the engine traces a margin/inventory mismanagement chain into solvency failure and distinguishes rebate-driven phantom 'profitability' from genuine demand-backed performance.
